cover.question: Why did they laugh at her?
cover.name: QUINTEN MASSYS
cover.work: An Old Woman (The Ugly Duchess), about 1513
cover.answered_by: Massys painted her as a satire: an old woman in the fashions of her youth, a low bodice and a rosebud held out to a man, mocking old people who dress and flirt as if still young (National Gallery)

facts.claim: Quinten Massys painted An Old Woman ('The Ugly Duchess') about 1513, oil on oak; it is in the National Gallery, London
It is a satirical portrait: with its pendant, An Old Man, it mocks old people who dress and behave as if they were still young
Her horned headdress and dress were the fashion of her youth, decades out of date by about 1513
She holds a red rosebud; in the pendant portrait she offers it to the old man, trying to win (seduce) him; the bud signalled she was seeking a suitor

Some doctors have suggested she had Paget's disease of bone (J. Dequeker, BMJ 1989; surgeon Michael Baum, 2008); the National Gallery thinks a folkloric, fictional figure more likely, so the narration says 'if they're right'
The painting (or a version of it) inspired John Tenniel's Duchess in Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865)

caption:
This woman was painted for people to laugh at.

Quinten Massys painted her in Antwerp around 1513. Look at her horned headdress and her dress: the fashion of her youth, decades out of date. Look at her low, tight bodice, a scandal at her age, and the red rosebud in her hand. She was half of a pair: in the matching portrait of an old man, she holds the bud out to him, trying to win him over. The pair mocked old people who dressed and flirted as if they were still young.

Now look at her face. In 1989 a doctor writing in the British Medical Journal suggested she had Paget's disease, a real condition that thickens and deforms the bones; surgeon Michael Baum made a similar case in 2008. The National Gallery thinks she is more likely a figure from carnival folklore. But if the doctors are right, the joke was on a sick woman.

Centuries later, her face inspired John Tenniel's Duchess in Alice in Wonderland (1865).

It hangs in the National Gallery, in London.

👁️ Would you have laughed?
